entry: 1953 dystopian novel by American writer [[Ray Bradbury]]. Set in a future America where books are outlawed, it follows Guy Montag, a fireman who burns books until he turns against censorship and begins preserving literature. Bradbury wrote it during the Second Red Scare, drawing on Nazi book burnings and ideological repression in the Soviet Union, but his accounts of its purpose changed over time; in later years he described it as a commentary on how mass media reduces interest in reading. The novel was censored in [[Apartheid|apartheid]] South Africa and in some U.S. schools. A 1966 film adaptation was directed by [[François Truffaut]].

Temperature scale proposed in 1724 by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit. Its lower reference point, 0 °F, was the freezing temperature of a [[Brine|brine]] of water, ice and [[Ammonium chloride|ammonium chloride]]; the upper point was his estimate of average human body temperature, first set at 90 °F and later at 96 °F. For much of the 20th century the scale was defined by water freezing at 32 °F and boiling at 212 °F at sea level and standard atmospheric pressure, a 180-degree interval. It is now defined through the [[Kelvin]] scale. Fahrenheit remains in use in the [[United States]] and its territories, Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and the [[Cayman Islands]]. Several other territories and nations use it alongside [[Celsius]], which was developed 18 years later and was called centigrade until 1948.

Twin-turbofan, single-seat [[Attack aircraft|attack aircraft]] built by Fairchild Republic for the U.S. Air Force, designed for close air support against armor. Built around a 30 mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon, it has 1,200 pounds (540 kg) of [[Titanium|titanium]] armor around its cockpit. In service since 1977, it has fought in the [[Gulf War]], the [[Yugoslav Wars]], the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|war in Afghanistan]], the [[Iraq War]] and the campaign against the [[Islamic State]]. Its planned replacement by the [[Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II]] remains contentious. Congress allowed retirements to begin in 2023, but further retirements were paused until the Air Force can show that its close-air-support role can be replaced.

Lebanese singer and symbol of modern Lebanon, widely considered one of the most celebrated vocalists in the [[Arab world]]. Born Nouhad Wadie Haddad, she began as a chorus singer at Lebanese national radio in the late 1940s, and her stage name is the Arabic word for [[Turquoise|turquoise]]. Her first major hit, "Itab", appeared in 1952. After her 1957 performance at the Baalbeck International Festival, Lebanese president Camille Chamoun awarded her the Cavalier medal, the highest honor for artistic achievement. Her fame spread through the 1950s and 1960s, bringing performances in [[Damascus]], [[Amman]] and [[Cairo]]. Over six decades she recorded nearly 1,500 songs, released more than 80 [[Album|albums]], performed in 20 musicals and sold over 150 million records.

Mythical being in the [[Folklore|folklore]] of several European cultures, usually humanlike and magical. Folk theories of its origin cast fairies as demoted angels or demons, pagan deities, spirits of the dead, prehistoric precursors to humans or spirits of nature, and some historians have linked them to the Persian peris. The label has been applied both to specific humanlike creatures with magical powers and a taste for trickery, and to any magical creature, such as goblins and gnomes. Church bells, clothing worn inside out and four-leaf clover were used as charms against them. Before modern medicine, fairies were often blamed for sickness, particularly [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] and birth deformities. They were popular in Renaissance literature and were especially fashionable in the [[United Kingdom]] during the Victorian and Edwardian eras.

Folklore [[Short story|short story]] typically featuring magic, enchantments and mythical or fanciful beings. Fairy tales are distinguished from legends, which are perceived as true within their culture, and from explicit moral tales such as [[Fable|beast fables]]. The term was first used by Madame d'Aulnoy in the late 17th century. Many tales are centuries old, and some may date back to the [[Bronze Age]], though often only literary forms survive. Literary collections by [[Charles Perrault]] (1697), the Brothers Grimm (1812) and [[Hans Christian Andersen]] (1835) shaped the modern genre. Folklorists classify tales by the Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index and the morphological analysis of Vladimir Propp.

King of Saudi Arabia (r. 1964–1975). As crown prince from 1953 he outlawed [[Slavery|slavery]] in the kingdom, and he pursued modernization and reform, including limits on the power of Islamic religious officials, though some of his reforms were controversial. His foreign policy emphasized pan-Islamism, [[Communism|anti-communism]], [[Zionism|anti-Zionism]] and pro-Palestinianism. In protest at Western support for Israel, he led the oil embargo that caused the [[1973 oil crisis]]. He was assassinated by a nephew in 1975 and succeeded by his half-brother Khalid.

Industrial city in [[Punjab]] province, Pakistan, and the province's second-largest city. Founded in the 1890s as a planned canal colony and named Lyallpur after the British lieutenant governor of the Punjab, Sir James Broadwood Lyall, it was one of the first planned cities in British India. Its centre was laid out with eight roads radiating from a clock tower, a design modeled on the [[Union Jack]]. It was renamed Faisalabad in 1979 in honor of King [[Faisal of Saudi Arabia|Faisal]]. Its population grew sixfold in the decade after partition as East Punjabi Muslim immigrants settled there. Textile manufacturing dominates its economy, and it is called the [[Manchester]] of Pakistan for its extensive textile industry. The city contributes over 20 percent of national GDP, and the 2023 census counted 3,691,999 residents in its municipal corporation area.

Belief in God or in the doctrines or teachings of [[Religion|religion]]. Religious people often understand faith as confidence based on a perceived degree of warrant or evidence, while skeptics tend to see it as belief without evidence. According to [[Thomas Aquinas]], faith is "an act of the intellect assenting to the truth at the command of the will." The English word derives from the Latin *fidēs*, meaning trust, confidence or belief. [[Christianity|Christian]] views vary: some see faith as being persuaded that something is true, while early Christians, according to Teresa Morgan, understood it as a relationship of trust that created community. Some hold that true faith produces good works, while others hold that faith in [[Jesus]] brings eternal life regardless. Pope Francis has claimed that most people on the planet profess to be believers.

American country singer and actress, one of the most successful country music artists of all time. Her first two albums, *Take Me as I Am* (1993) and *It Matters to Me* (1995), were major successes, and *Breathe* (1999) became one of the best-selling [[Country music|country]] albums of all time, winning three [[Grammy Awards]]. Hill has won five Grammys and 15 Academy of Country Music Awards. Her 2006 Soul2Soul II Tour with Tim McGraw became the highest-grossing country tour of all time. She has been married to McGraw since 1996.

South Korean professional [[League of Legends]] player, who has been the mid-laner for T1 throughout a career that began in 2013. He has won a record 10 LCK titles and a record six World Championships, including the 2023, 2024 and 2025 titles, and is widely regarded as the greatest player in the game's history. He has been compared to [[Michael Jordan]] for his esports success. He won a silver medal at the 2018 [[Asian Games]] and gold medals in 2022 and 2026 while representing South Korea. In 2020 he became a part-owner and executive of T1 Entertainment & Sports.

Deep-fried ball or patty of Egyptian origin, made from ground fava beans, [[Chickpea|chickpeas]] or both, mixed with herbs and spices. It is a popular street food throughout the [[Middle East]], most often made with fava beans in Egypt and the [[Arabian Peninsula]] and with chickpeas in the [[Levant]]. Falafel is often served in flatbread such as pita, topped with salads, pickled vegetables and hot sauce, and drizzled with tahini-based sauces. The word was first attested in English in 1936. Both sides in the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]] have claimed ownership of the dish.

Bird of prey in the genus *Falco*, which includes about 40 species. Falcons are found on every continent except [[Antarctica]]. Adults have thin, tapered wings that allow high speed and rapid changes of direction. Falcons kill prey with a tomial tooth on the beak, while hawks, [[Eagle|eagles]] and other birds of prey of the family Accipitridae use talons. The largest species is the gyrfalcon, up to 65 cm (26 in) long; the smallest is the Seychelles kestrel, at 15–24 cm. As with hawks and owls, females are typically larger than males. The [[Peregrine falcon]] has been recorded diving at 320 km/h (200 mph). The genus was introduced by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758, and falcons are not closely related to other birds of prey; their nearest relatives are [[Parrot|parrots]] and [[Songbird|songbirds]].

[[Archipelago]] (pop., 2021: 3,662) in the South Atlantic Ocean, a British Overseas Territory. The main islands lie about 500 km east of [[Patagonia]] and include East Falkland, where the capital, Stanley, is located, and West Falkland, with 776 smaller islands. The territory has internal self-government, while the United Kingdom is responsible for defense and foreign affairs. The economy rests on fishing, tourism and sheep farming, with wool exports. Argentina maintains a claim to sovereignty; British rule was reasserted in 1833, and Argentina's 1982 invasion prompted the [[Falklands War]]. In a 2013 referendum almost all votes cast favored remaining a UK overseas territory. Oil exploration remains controversial because of maritime disputes with Argentina.

Undeclared 1982 war between [[Argentina]] and the [[United Kingdom]] over the [[Falkland Islands]] and South Georgia. Argentina invaded the Falklands on 2 April 1982, and a British naval task force retook them. Argentina surrendered on 14 June after 74 days of conflict, which killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British personnel and three Falkland Islanders. The defeat hastened the fall of Argentina's military government. In Britain, the government of [[Margaret Thatcher]] was re-elected with a larger majority the following year. Diplomatic relations were restored in 1989, but the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

American rock band formed in 2001 in Wilmette, Illinois, a suburb of [[Chicago]]. Its 2005 album *From Under the Cork Tree* went double platinum and produced the hit singles "Sugar, We're Goin Down" and "Dance, Dance". *Infinity on High* (2007), *Save Rock and Roll* (2013), *American Beauty/American Psycho* (2015) and *Mania* (2018) each reached number one on the Billboard 200. The band received a Best New Artist nomination at the 2006 [[Grammy Awards]] and a Best Rock Album nomination for *Mania*.

Capture of [[Constantinople]], capital of the [[Byzantine Empire]], by the [[Ottoman Empire]] on 29 May 1453. The Ottoman army, which far outnumbered the defenders, was led by Sultan [[Mehmed II]]; the Byzantines were commanded by Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos. The 53-day [[Siege|siege]] began on 6 April. Ottoman cannons fired stone balls weighing 500 kilograms (1,100 lb) over the Theodosian walls, which had protected the city for about 800 years and created breaches for the assault. Mehmed II made Constantinople the Ottoman capital, replacing Adrianople, and the [[Hagia Sophia]] was converted into a mosque. The fall marked the effective end of the [[Roman Empire]], which had begun around 27 BC, and for many historians it marks the end of the [[Middle Ages]].

Capture of Saigon, capital of [[South Vietnam]], by North Vietnamese forces on 30 April 1975. The final assault followed a spring offensive by the People's Army of Vietnam and [[Viet Cong]] forces. In Operation Frequent Wind, the largest helicopter evacuation in history, almost all American personnel and tens of thousands of South Vietnamese were flown out. The fall ended the [[Vietnam War]] and the existence of South Vietnam. The country was formally reunified in 1976 with its capital in [[Hanoi]], and Saigon was renamed [[Ho Chi Minh City]].

End of Assadist rule in [[Syria]], on 8 December 2024. The collapse came during an offensive by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, the Syrian National Army and the Southern Operations Room, part of the [[Syrian civil war]]. The capture of [[Damascus]] ended a family rule that had governed Syria as a hereditary dictatorship since Hafez al-Assad seized power in a coup. Reports said [[Bashar al-Assad]] had fled to [[Russia]], where he was granted asylum, and the Russian government confirmed his resignation. Analysts viewed the collapse as a blow to Iran's Axis of Resistance, which had used Syria to supply arms to [[Hezbollah]].

Opening of the inner German border on 9 November 1989, which led to the dismantling of the [[Berlin Wall]]. A Politburo press conference prematurely announced that East Germans could travel without restriction, and crowds at border crossings eventually passed through as puzzled guards let them. Thousands crossed that night, and demolition followed. The event was part of the [[Revolutions of 1989]]: Hungary had opened its border in August, and [[Erich Honecker]], East Germany's long-term leader, was ousted in October. Free elections in spring 1990 showed preference for [[German reunification|reunification]], which took effect on 3 October 1990.

headword: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
sort_key: fall of the western roman empire
entry: Loss of central political control in the [[Western Roman Empire]], conventionally dated to 476. In 376 large numbers of [[Goths]] and other non-Roman peoples, fleeing the [[Huns]], entered the empire, and Roman forces could not expel or subjugate them. After [[Theodosius I]] died in 395, the empire was divided between the ministers of his two sons, and the Western armed forces became few and ineffective. In 476 the Germanic king Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and sent the imperial insignia to the Eastern emperor Zeno. The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire survived for centuries. Historians cite army strength, economic decline, imperial competence, internal struggles, religious change, disease and climate. [[Edward Gibbon]]'s 1776 history of the decline and fall of Rome shaped how the period is written about, and the period is also described as [[Late antiquity|late antiquity]], which emphasizes cultural continuity.

Invalid or faulty reasoning in the construction of an [[Argument|argument]] that may appear well-reasoned if unnoticed. The term was introduced in the Western tradition by [[Aristotle]] in *De Sophisticis Elenchis*. Fallacies may be used deliberately to persuade by deception, or arise through carelessness, cognitive bias or ignorance. A fallacy does not necessarily lead to a false conclusion; affirming the consequent is one example. Formal fallacies are flaws in the structure of a deductive argument, while informal fallacies arise from error in content or context and are frequently found in [[Mass media|mass media]]. A [[Mathematical proof|mathematical]] fallacy is an intentionally invalid proof, usually of an obvious contradiction, crafted for teaching.

House museum in Stewart Township, Pennsylvania, built partly over a waterfall on Bear Run. Designed by [[Frank Lloyd Wright]] as a weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr., owner of a [[Pittsburgh]] department store, it was commissioned in 1934 and occupied from 1937. Its cantilevered terraces extend from a [[Chimney|chimney]] and are built of local stone, reinforced concrete and steel. Sagging terraces and other structural defects required renovation in the late 1990s and early 2000s. The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has operated it as a museum since 1963. It is a National Historic Landmark and one of eight buildings in *The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright*, a [[World Heritage Site]].

American media franchise of post-apocalyptic role-playing video games, created by Tim Cain and Leonard Boyarsky at Interplay Entertainment. The series is set in the first half of the 3rd millennium, after a nuclear exchange between the United States and China. Its atompunk setting draws on the post-war culture of the 1950s United States. The series is regarded as a spiritual successor to the 1988 game *Wasteland*. The first title, *Fallout*, was released in 1997, followed by *Fallout 3* in 2008, *Fallout: New Vegas* in 2010, *Fallout 4* in 2015 and *Fallout 76* in 2018.

New religious movement founded in China in 1992 by Li Hongzhi, combining qigong exercises and meditation with Buddhist and [[Tao|Taoist]] moral teachings. Adherents practice five exercises, and the movement claims that its practices can cure illness without modern medicine. In July 1999 the Chinese government banned it as an illegal organization; [[Human rights|human rights]] groups have documented mass arrests and torture of practitioners. Its global headquarters is in Deerpark, New York. Its media arm, which publishes *The Epoch Times*, has been described as far-right and criticized for promoting conspiracy theories.
